text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--- Within recent years public sector employees have had the lowest salary rises in Denmark, but total salary expenses per public employee are still higher than salary expenses in the private sector and the government is therefore wants to keep public sector wages down in 1997.

--- The family conflict in Scandinavia's largest weekly magazine group Aller is now official with a group of minority shareholders within the family demanding an end to the rules limiting the sale of A- shares to family members only. The minority accuses the majority group of using its board dominance to vote itself high salaries and pensions.

--- Finance minister Mogens Lykketoft is to lead a trade delegation to Pakistan in May, hoping to boost exports of agricultural and fishing products, power stations and consultancy services in connection with the building of a new Pakistani infrastructure.

--- Immigrants' Danish language skills are too poor, a new education ministry report on almost half of Denmark's 40,000 immigrants shows. The ministry therefore plans a new and better one-year training programme for Danish language teachers to improve present levels.
--- A parliament majority favours church plans to allow the marriage of homosexual couples.
--- Denmark's largest shipyard, Lindoevaerftet, is developing new types of ships to replace present container ships, but has not yet decided which type of ship to aim for in future.

--- The Radical Liberals are demanding extensive structural reform, including a rise in the average age for receiving state pensions, if they are to remain as coalition partners to the Social Democrats after the 1998 general election.

---The opposition Conservatives refuse to back the present government's plans for welfare reform, saying that they prefer to make a clean start as part of a Lberal/Conservative government after the 1998 elections.
--- The Radical Liberals warn that Social Democrat plans to push for tougher prison sentences could force them to quit the coalition.
